statement:
In people aged 12 and older, mostly young to middle-aged adults in New Zealand, the United States and Ontario, many of whom also smoked tobacco, smoking cannabis (self-reported; mostly light or infrequent in CARDIA, the long US cohort, and in the Ontario cohort) compared with not smoking cannabis is associated with more cough, phlegm, wheeze and bronchitis episodes. In CARDIA, lung function was not lower at light cumulative exposure, and in the Ontario cohort respiratory emergency visits and admissions over 12 months were not more frequent; what heavy smoking over many years does to lung function is not known. The evidence is a 2018 systematic review of 22 studies, CARDIA (5,115 adults followed 20 years), the Ontario record-linkage cohort (12 months of follow-up) and the 2017 National Academies committee's review (a narrative review, read here for its conclusions and the studies under them). The systematic review and the committee draw on some of the same cohorts (CARDIA, Dunedin, Los Angeles), so they are not independent confirmations of each other.

Symptoms. In the review's pooled comparisons of people who smoked cannabis with people who used neither cannabis nor tobacco, 4 cross-sectional studies gave risk ratios of 4.37 (95% CI 1.71–11.19) for cough, 3.40 (1.99–5.79) for phlegm and 2.83 (1.89–4.23) for wheeze, and 2 prospective cohorts (Dunedin, followed 15 years on average, and Los Angeles, 9.8 years with 49% lost to follow-up) gave 2.04 (1.02–4.06) for cough and 3.84 (1.62–9.07) for phlegm; these two pooled estimates were not significant after the review's small-sample adjustment (P = 0.10 and 0.20), although its abstract reports the intervals as showing an increased risk. The Los Angeles cohort found more bronchitis episodes (odds ratio 2.3, 1.2–4.4), and both cohorts found fewer symptoms after people stopped. In a convenience sample of 339 people in Wellington (the committee's account), cough was reported by 29% of people who smoked cannabis against 5% of people who did not, wheeze by 27% against 11% and chronic bronchitis symptoms by 19% against 3%. The committee graded the evidence for an association between long-term cannabis smoking and worse symptoms and more bronchitis episodes 'substantial', and for improvement after stopping 'moderate' (its wording; mostly cross-sectional studies and two cohorts, with self-reported use, incomplete control for tobacco and, in one cohort, high loss to follow-up). The review rated its own evidence for cough, phlegm and wheeze 'low'.

Lung function. In CARDIA (5,115 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start; spirometry at years 0, 2, 5, 10 and 20; 69% still taking part at year 20; use mostly light, a median of 2 to 3 episodes in the past 30 days among people who smoked cannabis), with tobacco counted in the same model, people currently smoking cannabis only did not differ from people smoking neither (FEV1 +0.7 mL, 95% CI −12 to 13), and more lifetime exposure up to about 7 joint-years (one joint-year is 365 joints) went with slightly higher, not lower, FEV1 (net +53 mL, 28 to 79) and FVC (+64 mL, 36 to 92) than none. Beyond that the estimates were imprecise and flattened or turned negative (FEV1 +27 mL, −10 to 64, at 20 joint-years; −39 mL, −141 to 64, at 50), from few people with heavy cannabis exposure and no tobacco (40 with more than 20 joint-years). Other cohorts were not uniform: Dunedin (10 years) found no change in FEV1 and Los Angeles (8 years) no significant fall, while Tucson (4 to 5 cannabis cigarettes a week) found lower FEV1 after 1 year. The review rated the evidence on FEV1, FVC and the FEV1/FVC ratio 'insufficient'. The committee rated the evidence of higher FVC 'moderate' and wrote that it is unclear whether cannabis smoking is associated with worse lung function; it also graded the evidence on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in people who smoke cannabis occasionally when tobacco was controlled for 'limited', on admissions for COPD 'insufficient' and on asthma 'no or insufficient'.

Hospital use. In an Ontario record-linkage cohort (4,807 people aged 12 to 65 who had used cannabis in the past year, 42.5% of them less than monthly, matched to 10,395 who had not; 73.9% of both groups currently or formerly smoking tobacco; 12 months of follow-up, data before October 2018), respiratory emergency visits or admissions were 3.6% against 3.9% (odds ratio 0.91, 0.77–1.09), while emergency visits or admissions for any reason were 30.0% against 26.0% (1.22, 1.13–1.31). The respiratory odds ratio was 0.80 (0.65–0.99) among people who currently or formerly smoked tobacco and 1.23 (0.89–1.70) among people who had never smoked tobacco or had no record, uncorrected subgroup tests. Exposure was one question about any use in the past year; route, amount and strength were not collected.

Tobacco and the comparison. Tobacco was common in these groups (73.9% in the Ontario groups; a 2018 commentary cites about 70% of people who use cannabis also smoking tobacco and notes that cannabis is often combined with tobacco in cannabis cigarettes). Many symptom studies did not control for it (the committee), and NHANES and SPIROMICS reported FEV1 only for cannabis and tobacco smoking together, so a difference from people who smoke neither can partly reflect tobacco; the commentary adds that statistically controlling for tobacco may remove variance that belongs to cannabis use. Where tobacco was counted in the same model (CARDIA), tobacco alone showed the expected dose-related loss (FEV1 63 mL lower, −89 to −36, at more than 20 cigarettes a day) and no significant interaction between tobacco and cannabis was found for FEV1 or FVC; the committee notes no clear additive effect of smoking both on symptoms (one cross-sectional study). Whether tobacco was mixed into joints was not recorded in CARDIA or the Ontario data.

Against tobacco. The committee's chapter summary says the respiratory risks of cannabis smoking appear relatively small and far lower than those of tobacco smoking, a judgment that is not one of its numbered conclusions. Its chapter also reports pieces that point the other way: in 15 volunteers one joint gave about four times the carbon monoxide and three to five times the tar deposition of one cigarette, and in the Wellington sample the authors estimated that each joint's association with a lower FEV1/FVC ratio was similar to that of 2.5 to 5 cigarettes (an analysis the committee criticises); it adds that people who smoke cannabis usually smoke fewer per day. No study in the parts read compared the two at matched exposure.

Not measured and limits. Cannabis use was self-reported; route and method of smoking (joint, pipe, bong), amount, product strength and tobacco mixed into joints were not recorded in CARDIA or the Ontario data, and the committee notes that a joint's strength varies widely between joints and between years. Cohorts were young, and the review's authors note that obstructive lung disease in people who smoke tobacco is usually identified after age 35 to 40. None of these studies can show cause. The only comparison with another way of taking cannabis in the parts read is a 12-person study without a control group, in which symptoms resolved about a month after people switched from smoking to a vaporizer (the committee's account); the committee lists whether other inhaled forms cause fewer respiratory symptoms as unknown. Funding as printed: the review, no project funding (two authors with federal support); the CARDIA analysis, the US National Institute on Drug Abuse (CARDIA's data collection is funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute); the Ontario study, a grant competition run by The Lung Association – Ontario with unrestricted funding from Tetra-Bio Pharma, a company developing cannabinoid drugs (the paper says the funders had no role); the committee's report, US federal agencies and health foundations, with no cannabis or tobacco industry sponsor listed. The Ontario result (no extra respiratory visits) is paired with independent work: the 20-year CARDIA cohort found no sign of harm to lung function at light exposure, while the independent review found more symptoms. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed (the symptom finding alone would be replicated; the lung-function findings are mixed).
plain: In studies that compared people who smoke cannabis with people who do not, people who smoked cannabis more often had cough, phlegm and wheezing, and in two long-running studies these eased in people who stopped. Many of the people who smoked cannabis also smoked tobacco, so the studies cannot say how much of this comes from cannabis. In the longest study (5,115 adults followed for 20 years; those who smoked cannabis mostly did so lightly), lung function was not lower in people who smoked cannabis lightly, while tobacco smoking lowered it; too few people had smoked cannabis heavily for many years to know what that does. An Ontario study that followed about 15,000 people for a year found no difference in emergency visits or hospital stays for breathing problems between people who had used cannabis and people who had not, although it counted any use and most people used it infrequently. None of this shows what smoking cannabis itself does. The only comparison with another way of taking cannabis was one small study of 12 people with no comparison group, in which symptoms eased about a month after a switch from smoking to a vaporizer.
population: People aged 12 and older, mostly young to middle-aged adults, in New Zealand, the United States and Ontario (Canada); cannabis smoking self-reported, mostly light or infrequent in the long US cohort and the Ontario cohort and moderate to heavy in the pooled cross-sectional symptom studies and the Los Angeles cohort; many also smoked tobacco
exposure: Smoking cannabis, self-reported (joints, pipes or bongs; method, amount, strength and any tobacco mixed in mostly not recorded)
comparator: People who do not smoke cannabis: in the pooled symptom comparisons, people who used neither cannabis nor tobacco; in the 20-year US cohort, people with no cannabis exposure, with tobacco counted separately in the same model; in the Ontario cohort, matched people who had not used cannabis in the past year (73.9% of both groups currently or formerly smoking tobacco). For tobacco: people who smoked tobacco only (CARDIA)
outcome: Cough, phlegm, wheeze and bronchitis episodes; lung function (FEV1 and FVC) over time; emergency visits and admissions for respiratory reasons
magnitude: Symptoms, people who smoked cannabis against people who used neither cannabis nor tobacco (2018 review; risk ratio, 95% CI; risk difference): 4 cross-sectional studies pooled: cough 4.37 (1.71–11.19; 0.18, 0.15–0.21), phlegm 3.40 (1.99–5.79; 0.14, 0.10–0.17), wheeze 2.83 (1.89–4.23; 0.22, 0.14–0.29), dyspnea 1.56 (1.33–1.83; 0.06, −0.01 to 0.13); the risk differences are weighted differently from the ratios and mostly reflect one or two large studies. 2 prospective cohorts pooled (Dunedin, Los Angeles): cough 2.04 (1.02–4.06; 0.07, 0.02–0.13) and phlegm 3.84 (1.62–9.07; 0.12, −0.02 to 0.25), not significant after the small-sample adjustment (P = 0.10, 0.20). Los Angeles cohort: bronchitis episodes OR 2.3 (1.2–4.4). Wellington sample of 339 (committee's account): cough 29% against 5%, wheeze 27% against 11%, chronic bronchitis symptoms 19% against 3%. Committee's grades (its wording): 'substantial' for the association of long-term smoking with worse symptoms and more bronchitis episodes; 'moderate' for improvement after stopping. Lung function (CARDIA, tobacco in the same model; net difference against no exposure): lifetime cannabis exposure FEV1 +53 mL (28 to 79) and FVC +64 mL (36 to 92) at 7 joint-years; FEV1 +27 mL (−10 to 64) at 20 and −39 mL (−141 to 64) at 50; currently smoking cannabis only against neither FEV1 +0.7 mL (−12 to 13), FVC +8.2 mL (−5 to 22); tobacco only FEV1 −24 mL (−38 to −11). Ontario, matched, 12 months: respiratory emergency visit or admission 3.6% against 3.9%, OR 0.91 (0.77–1.09); any reason 30.0% against 26.0%, OR 1.22 (1.13–1.31).

evidence.locator: Methods › Study Selection; Results › Literature Search; Results › Study Characteristics
evidence.extracted: Registered review (PROSPERO CRD42017059224): 22 studies (10 prospective cohort, 12 cross-sectional) out of 73 candidate articles; 3 rated high risk of bias. Five databases, 1 January 1973 to 30 April 2018, English only; people older than 12 years with at least 30 days of lifetime cannabis use. 13 distinct outcomes, 5 poolable. Every exposure described is smoking (joints, joint-years); methods of quantifying use varied (monthly, weekly or daily use; joint-years; cigarette-years).

evidence.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend
evidence.extracted: Prospective cohorts, 2 studies pooled (Dunedin cohort, n = 1037, mean follow-up 15 years, use about once a week for a year on average; Los Angeles cohort, 299 people, mean 3.0 joints a day for 9.8 years, 49% lost to follow-up), people who used cannabis against people who did not: cough RR 2.04 (95% CI 1.02 to 4.06), RD 0.07 (0.02 to 0.13); sputum production RR 3.84 (1.62 to 9.07), RD 0.12 (-0.02 to 0.25); heterogeneity low. After the Knapp-Hartung adjustment the pooled RRs were not significant (cough P = 0.10; sputum P = 0.20). Both studies found that stopping cannabis was followed by a significant fall in respiratory symptoms. The abstract and Results report the pooled intervals (which exclude 1) as showing an increased risk; the Figure 2 legend gives the Knapp-Hartung P values.

evidence.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Single prospective studies not pooled: the Tucson random-sample cohort (n = 1802, four surveys 1981 to 1988, moderate risk of bias) found current cannabis smoking associated with chronic cough OR 1.73 (1.21 to 2.47), chronic sputum OR 1.53 (1.08 to 2.18) and wheezing OR 2.01 (1.50 to 2.70); the Dunedin study found wheezing OR 1.55 (1.23 to 1.94), P < 0.001, and a trend for dyspnea OR 1.23 (0.97 to 1.56), P = 0.086.

evidence.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 legend; Table (wheezing comment); Discussion, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Cross-sectional studies, 4 pooled (1 low and 3 moderate risk of bias; all included moderate to heavy use), people who used cannabis against people who did not: cough RR 4.37 (1.71 to 11.19), RD 0.18 (0.15 to 0.21); sputum production RR 3.40 (1.99 to 5.79), RD 0.14 (0.10 to 0.17); wheezing RR 2.83 (1.89 to 4.23), RD 0.22 (0.14 to 0.29); dyspnea RR 1.56 (1.33 to 1.83), RD 0.06 (-0.01 to 0.13). Knapp-Hartung P: cough 0.05, sputum 0.05, wheezing 0.01, dyspnea below 0.01. Heterogeneity was high for wheezing and is attributed to non-uniform exposure and symptom definitions. The pooled risk differences are weighted differently from the ratios (for dyspnea the ratio's interval excludes 1 while the difference's includes 0) and mostly reflect one or two large studies, so they are not typical figures; which four studies were pooled is shown only in a forest-plot image, which was not read.

evidence.locator: Results › Obstructive Lung Disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 3 legend
evidence.extracted: Chronic bronchitis and COPD: the Los Angeles cohort (3.0 joints a day, mean 9.8 years, 49% lost) found more bronchitis episodes, OR 2.3 (1.2 to 4.4), P = 0.011. Three cross-sectional studies pooled: RR 2.28 (0.68 to 7.72), RD 0.06 (-0.04 to 0.16), not significant (Knapp-Hartung P = 0.31). SPIROMICS (n = 1174, people currently or formerly smoking tobacco only): current use OR 0.87 (0.59 to 1.31), former use OR 1.0 (0.79 to 1.26). A high-risk-of-bias study found COPD prevalence higher by 0.3% (0.0% to 0.5%) per joint-year, with people who used cannabis and tobacco combined.

evidence.locator: Results › Change in Pulmonary Function › FEV1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; FVC, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: FEV1: CARDIA (rated low risk of bias; 5115 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start): current use, adjusted mean difference −18 mL (−42 to 6.1); a Los Angeles cohort (mean age 33, over 3.5 joints a day, 8 years): no significant fall in people who smoked cannabis continuously or intermittently against people who did not smoke it; Dunedin (10 years): no change. FVC: CARDIA lifetime use over 10 joint-years +59 mL (12 to 107); cross-sectional SPIROMICS higher FVC in current and former use and NHANES +0.07% per joint-year (NHANES and SPIROMICS reported FEV1 only for cannabis and tobacco smoking combined). The review describes the CARDIA −18 mL as minimal exposure and attaches trend P values (0.32, 0.03, 0.01) to single contrasts; in the primary paper the −18 mL contrast is the heaviest current category and those P values are for trend, so CARDIA is cited from the primary paper (anchors below).

evidence.locator: Results › Change in Pulmonary Function › FEV1, 2nd paragraph; FEV1-FVC Ratio, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › Airway Resistance and Specific Conductance of Airways
evidence.extracted: Tucson (4 to 5 cannabis cigarettes a week, moderate risk of bias): significant FEV1 reductions after 1 year (P < 0.01) and a significant reduction in the FEV1-FVC ratio. NHANES 2007 to 2010 (low risk of bias): more than 20 joint-years against people who did not smoke cannabis, ratio below 70%, OR 2.1 (1.1 to 3.9) after tobacco adjustment (the earlier NHANES study, moderate risk of bias: no definite relationship); SPIROMICS (mean 30.1 joint-years, all with a tobacco-smoking history): positive association with a low ratio, P < 0.001; a Wellington study (n = 339, mean 54.2 joint-years) marginally lower ratio, −1.1% (−2.6% to 0.1%). All four studies of airway resistance and specific conductance (1 prospective, low risk of bias; 3 cross-sectional) found higher resistance and lower conductance in people who smoked cannabis.

evidence.locator: Results › Strength of Evidence; Table
evidence.extracted: Strength of evidence (AHRQ method): low for cough, sputum production, wheezing and airway resistance; insufficient for dyspnea, obstructive lung disease, FEV1, FVC, FEV1-FVC ratio and other respiratory outcomes.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph; Results › Study Characteristics
evidence.extracted: The authors say the lung-function evidence is limited by low exposure and young cohorts: tobacco's effect on FEV1 becomes measurable only after about 5 to 10 pack-years; obstructive lung disease develops in about a third of people who smoke tobacco long term and is usually identified after age 35 to 40; large cohorts of middle-aged to older people with heavier cannabis exposure may be needed. They add, as a conjecture, that few people may use enough cannabis to change lung function, so lung function may not be among its most important long-term health outcomes. Across all prospective lung-function evaluations only 243 people (131 cannabis-only) had more than 20 joint-years; the authors also count 756 people who smoked cannabis only with more than 20 joint-years across all outcomes and studies (a different scope).

evidence.locator: Methods › Study Design and Sample; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1; Abstract (Results)
evidence.extracted: 5115 adults aged 18 to 30 were recruited in 1985 to 1986 in four US cities; spirometry at years 0, 2, 5, 10 and 20 with 69% retention at year 20. Of 20,777 visits with spirometry, 19,703 (95%) from 5016 participants (98%) were used, 3.9 visits each on average; attrition was more common in people who smoked tobacco and not associated with cannabis use. 54% reported current cannabis or tobacco smoking, or both, at one or more exams (neither 2305, tobacco only 851, cannabis only 795, both 1065). Cannabis exposure was nearly as common as tobacco but mostly light: median 2 to 3 episodes in the past 30 days against 8 to 9 cigarettes a day for tobacco; 91 participants had no tobacco exposure and more than 10 joint-years of cannabis (153 spirometry observations), 40 of them more than 20 joint-years (56 observations).

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: One model with all four smoking variables (current and lifetime cannabis and tobacco). Cannabis, four-level categories, tobacco in the same model: lifetime exposure was associated with higher FVC and FEV1 than zero exposure (1 to 5 joint-years FEV1 +38 mL, 15 to 62; FVC +41 mL, 14 to 67; 6 to 10 joint-years FEV1 +66 mL, 32 to 100; FVC +54 mL, 16 to 91; over 10 joint-years FEV1 +36 mL, -6.5 to 79; FVC +59 mL, 12 to 107). Current heavy use (over 20 episodes in the past 30 days) was FEV1 -18 mL (-42 to 6.1) and FVC +20 mL (-5.2 to 49); people who used cannabis only differed little from people using neither (FEV1 +0.7 mL, -12 to 13; FVC +8.2 mL, -5 to 22), while tobacco only was -24 mL (-38 to -11) for FEV1. The Results text gives the top lifetime category as 'more than 20' joint-years while Table 2 labels it 'more than 10'; Table 2's label is used.

evidence.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 3 (lifetime marijuana rows); Abstract (Results)
evidence.extracted: Cannabis, spline models: the association with lifetime exposure was non-linear (P < 0.001 for FEV1 and FVC). The slope was +13 mL per joint-year for FEV1 (6.4 to 20) and +20 mL for FVC (12 to 27) at 2 joint-years, about zero at 7 joint-years (FEV1 -0.4, -2.6 to 1.8; FVC 0.0, -2.4 to 2.5), and for FEV1 -2.2 mL per joint-year (-4.6 to 0.3, P = 0.079) at 20 and 50 joint-years. Net FEV1 difference against no exposure: +53 mL (28 to 79) at 7 joint-years, +27 mL (-10 to 64) at 20 and -39 mL (-141 to 64) at 50; net FVC +64 (36 to 92), +76 (34 to 117) and +104 (-12 to 220). The Results text gives the interval of the −2.2 slope as −4.9 to 0.36 against −4.6 to 0.3 in the abstract and Table 3; neither is significant.

evidence.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 3 (current marijuana rows)
evidence.extracted: Current intensity, spline models: non-linear for both outcomes (FEV1 P = 0.025, FVC P = 0.035). At 20 episodes a month the FEV1 slope was -3.2 mL per episode a month (-5.8 to -0.6, P = 0.017) and the FVC slope -1.5 (-4.2 to 1.3); net differences at 20 episodes a month were FEV1 +14 mL (-4.7 to 32) and FVC +43 mL (23 to 63). No data at 40 episodes a month. The authors state the net FEV1 association became negative only at very high exposure (over 40 joint-years or 25 episodes a month) and not significantly.

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2; Table 3 (lifetime tobacco rows)
evidence.extracted: Tobacco (positive control): current smoking of more than 20 cigarettes a day was associated with FEV1 63 mL lower (95% CI -89 to -36) and FVC 69 mL lower (-97 to -41); lifetime exposure over 20 pack-years with FEV1 101 mL lower (-136 to -65). In spline models the association was linear and dose-related, with a slope of -7.0 mL per pack-year (-10 to -3.7) at 7 pack-years and net differences at 50 pack-years of -332 mL (-401 to -263) for FEV1 and -229 mL (-310 to -147) for FVC. No statistically significant interaction between tobacco and cannabis exposure was found for FEV1 or FVC.

evidence.locator: Comment, 1st paragraph; Comment, 6th to 8th paragraphs; final paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors conclude that up to about 7 joint-years of lifetime exposure (for example 1 joint a day for 7 years or 1 joint a week for 49 years) gave no evidence that more exposure harms lung function, that at higher exposure the pattern levelled off or reversed especially for FEV1, and that the sample contained too few people with heavy use to confirm a harmful effect of very heavy use. They propose a stretch or training effect (one version called a speculative possibility) and a short-lived airway widening, which they consider unlikely to explain the higher volumes. Limitations named by the authors: no plethysmography, diffusing capacity or imaging of emphysema; only a minority with very high cannabis exposure, fewer still without tobacco, so estimates at high exposure are imprecise; self-reported exposure with recall error and no record of smoking method; unmeasured confounding possible. The final paragraph says the findings suggest an accelerated decline with heavy use, but the net FEV1 differences at 20 and 50 joint-years and the spline slope (−2.2 mL per joint-year, P = 0.079) were not significant; only the slope for current use at 20 episodes a month was (−3.2 mL per episode a month, P = 0.017).

evidence.locator: Results › Cohort derivation, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Methods › Data sources; Discussion, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Of 35,114 Ontario residents aged 12 to 65 in the CCHS who either used cannabis in the past year or were controls, 6425 (18.3%) used cannabis in the past year; 4807 of them (74.8%) were matched to 10,395 controls (15,202 people). After matching, 73.9% of both groups currently or formerly smoked tobacco and standardised differences were below 0.10 for all variables. Cannabis use frequency in the matched cannabis group: less than once a month 42.5%, 1 to 3 times a month 18.1%, once a week 9.4%, more than once a week 11.4%, every day 10.5%, unknown 8.0%. Route, amount and potency were not collected; the authors say inhalation is by far the most common route (citing a scoping review).

evidence.locator: Results › Overall cohort analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Primary outcome, respiratory-related ER visit or hospital admission within 12 months: 175 events (3.6%) in the cannabis group against 410 (3.9%) in controls, OR 0.91 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.09), p = 0.32. All-cause ER visit or admission: 1443 (30.0%) against 2699 (26.0%), OR 1.22 (1.13 to 1.31), number needed to harm 25. All-cause death: 11 against 24 (0.2% each), OR 0.99 (0.49 to 2.02).

evidence.locator: Results › Sensitivity analyses › By sex; By tobacco smoking history; By pre-existing asthma or COPD; Table 4
evidence.extracted: Respiratory outcome by tobacco history: people currently or formerly smoking tobacco OR 0.80 (0.65 to 0.99), p = 0.04 (123 events, 3.5%, against 290, 4.2%); people who had never smoked tobacco or had no record OR 1.23 (0.89 to 1.70). All-cause outcome: 1.16 (1.06 to 1.26) and 1.35 (1.16 to 1.56). By sex, respiratory OR 1.00 (0.77 to 1.31) in men and 0.86 (0.68 to 1.10) in women; by pre-existing asthma or COPD, respiratory OR 0.82 (0.61 to 1.11) with and 0.96 (0.77 to 1.20) without. One row of Table 4 is internally inconsistent (events in the cannabis group 149 + 33 = 182, not the 175 of Table 2); people with missing tobacco status are analysed with people who never smoked tobacco.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors give reasons the null respiratory result may understate an effect (not adjustable): too little cannabis smoke exposure among people in the study (citing research that lung-function decline occurs only above 20 'joints per year'), some non-inhaled use, secondhand cannabis smoke in controls, and low power. They also say the large share of people in the cannabis group who used it infrequently may have contributed to the null result, that causation should not be inferred, and that unmeasured confounding might explain the positive findings. Limitations stated: self-report (recall and social-desirability bias); no dose-response (frequency categories too small); no quantity or potency data; about 25% of the cannabis group unmatched; data only before October 2018; no secondhand-smoke adjustment; too few people under 20 and aged 50 to 65 for age-group analyses; a single province. The Discussion's threshold of 20 joints per year for lung-function decline is the wrong unit (CARDIA uses joint-years) and a threshold the cited cohort did not establish.

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › Respiratory Symptoms, Including Chronic Bronchitis › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Hancox 2015, Walden and Earleywine, Tashkin 2012); Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Conclusion 7-3
evidence.extracted: Respiratory symptoms (Conclusion 7-3): the committee graded as substantial the evidence of a statistical association (7-3a) between long-term cannabis smoking and worse respiratory symptoms and more frequent chronic bronchitis episodes, and as moderate the evidence of an association (7-3b) between stopping and improvement. Under it: a 2007 systematic review of 14 symptom studies (nine cross-sectional, three case series, one case-control, one cohort; cough OR 1.7 to 2.0, sputum 1.5 to 1.9, wheeze 2.0 to 3.0); the Wellington cross-sectional study (cough 29% against 5%, wheeze 27% against 11%, chronic bronchitis symptoms 19% against 3%, people who smoked cannabis against people who did not); the Dunedin cohort of 1,037 followed to age 38 (frequent use, defined as 52 or more times in the past year: morning cough OR 1.97, sputum 2.31, wheeze 1.55; fewer symptoms after quitting); an internet survey of 5,987 adults recruited through drug-policy-reform organisations; a longitudinal cohort of 299 followed for at least two visits over 9.8 years, with high or variable loss to follow-up (current against never use: cough OR 1.7, sputum 2.1, bronchitis episodes 2.3, wheeze 3.4; current against former use: cough 3.3, sputum 4.2, wheeze 2.1). The committee notes no clear additive effect of smoking both cannabis and tobacco on symptoms.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › Respiratory Symptoms › Primary Studies (paragraphs after Figure 7-1 on Hancox 2015 limitations and on Walden and Earleywine); Discussion of Findings, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Limits of the symptom evidence as the committee states them: most studies relied on self-reported cannabis smoking; many did not control for tobacco and occupational or environmental exposures, or for dose or duration; joint-years were rarely used and the THC content of a joint varies widely between joints and between years; Dunedin classed fewer than 52 uses a year as non-use and did not know whether cannabis was smoked; the internet survey recruited through organisations advocating drug-policy reform.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › Pulmonary Function › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Papatheodorou, Pletcher, Hancox 2010, Van Dam and Earleywine); Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-1; Chapter Highlights
evidence.extracted: Lung function (Conclusion 7-1): 'moderate evidence' of an association between cannabis smoking and improved airway dynamics with acute use but not chronic use (7-1a) and with higher FVC (7-1b); the chapter highlight says it is unclear whether cannabis use is associated with worsened lung function. Under it: the 2007 review (34 publications; acute bronchodilation; regular smoking associated with lower specific airway conductance, about 16% on average, and a lower FEV1; inconsistent findings otherwise); CARDIA, 5,115 adults over 20 years, occasional and low cumulative smoking not associated with adverse effects on lung function, with a trend to lower FEV1 only at the heaviest exposure (20 or more joint-years) and with few people at heavy exposure; Dunedin (1,037, spirometry at 32): cumulative cannabis associated with higher FVC, total lung capacity and residual volume but not lower FEV1 or FEV1/FVC; NHANES 2007 to 2012 (10,327 adults, cross-sectional): lower FEV1/FVC and higher FEV1 and FVC in people who had smoked cannabis recently; a 12-person vaporizer feasibility study with no control group.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › Pulmonary Function › Primary Studies, paragraph on Aldington et al. (2007)
evidence.extracted: Wellington sample (Aldington et al., 2007; convenience sample of 339; entry required at least 5 joint-years of cannabis or 1 pack-year of tobacco, according to what was smoked; self-reported use): no association between long-term cannabis smoking and the lung-function variables in the main analysis, but per joint-year a significantly lower FEV1/FVC, lower specific airways conductance and higher total lung capacity than in people who did not smoke; the authors estimated that each joint's association with a lower FEV1/FVC was similar to that of 2.5 to 5 tobacco cigarettes. The committee criticises the analysis: only main effects were reported (no test of interaction between cannabis and tobacco) and coefficients were labelled odds ratios in two tables. The committee cites the same paper for the symptom percentages.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Tan 2009, Yadavilli, Macleod, Kempker); Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-2
evidence.extracted: COPD (Conclusion 7-2): 'limited evidence' of an association between occasional cannabis smoking and developing COPD when controlled for tobacco (7-2a); 'insufficient evidence' for hospital admissions for COPD (7-2b). Under it: a 339-person Wellington CT study with inconsistent results; Vancouver cross-sectional study of 878 adults (at least 50 cannabis cigarettes and no tobacco history: not at significantly greater risk of COPD or more respiratory symptoms; tobacco plus cannabis not clearly different from tobacco only); a 709-person readmission study (cannabis 0.22 against tobacco 0.26, unit not specified); a 500-person cross-sectional study with no non-smoking group (COPD 24.3% tobacco only against 25.2% tobacco plus cannabis, p = 0.90; more cough, phlegm and wheeze with both, no adjusted comparison); NHANES (more than 20 joint-years, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.1 to 3.9, but higher FVC and no FEV1 association, and pre-bronchodilator spirometry). The Discussion says it is unclear whether regular use is associated with developing or worsening COPD and cites a position statement of minimal impairment in people who smoke cannabis occasionally once tobacco is controlled for. The basis for the word occasional in Conclusion 7-2(a) is not apparent in the text read: the studies described do not show an association in people who smoke cannabis occasionally.

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › Asthma › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies; Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-4
evidence.extracted: Asthma (Conclusion 7-4): no or insufficient evidence to support or refute an association between cannabis smoking and asthma development or exacerbation, from a 506-boy cohort that found no link to self-reported asthma symptoms, a cohort of 110 adolescents with asthma that found no association with asthma concern, severity or symptoms, and one case-control letter of 100 emergency department patients that found no association with THC. The Discussion adds that wheeze appears common among people who use cannabis.

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › Respiratory Symptoms › Primary Studies, paragraph on Van Dam and Earleywine; Pulmonary Function › Primary Studies, paragraph on Van Dam and Earleywine; Respiratory Symptoms › Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Research Gaps
evidence.extracted: Van Dam and Earleywine (2010), as the committee describes it: 12 adults; switching from smoking cannabis to a vaporizer was correlated with resolution of cannabis-related respiratory symptoms, and with improved forced expiratory volumes, about 1 month later; no control group. The committee lists as unknown whether other inhaled forms of cannabis cause fewer respiratory symptoms and asks for trials of them against smoking.

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › Summary, 1st paragraph; Research Gaps, 1st paragraph and bullets
evidence.extracted: Chapter 7 Summary and gaps: the committee judges the respiratory risks of cannabis smoking to be relatively small and well below those of tobacco smoking; it says people who smoke heavily may be at higher risk of chronic bronchitis and COPD but that current studies do not give enough evidence of a link; and it names the limitations (cannabis and tobacco hard to separate; self-reported exposure; few cohorts of people who smoke regularly or daily; inadequate control of environmental factors; generalisability). Unknown, it says: whether long-term cannabis smoking above tobacco causes faster lung-function decline, chronic bronchitis or COPD; whether it raises the risk of allergic disease or asthma; whether other inhaled forms cause fewer respiratory symptoms. The tobacco comparison is the committee's overall judgment in the Summary, not a numbered conclusion; the chapter holds pieces pointing both ways and the sections read give no study comparing the two at matched exposure.

evidence.quote: appear to be relatively small and to be far lower than those of tobacco smoking

evidence.locator: Chapter 7 › opening text (before Pulmonary Function), 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Background given for smoke exposure: in 15 volunteers one cannabis joint gave about four times the carbon monoxide exposure and three to five times the tar deposition of a single cigarette, with deeper inhalation, longer breath-holding and no filters; against this, cannabis cigarettes are less densely packed and people who use cannabis usually smoke fewer of them per day than people who smoke tobacco smoke cigarettes.

evidence.locator: Appendix B › Data Synthesis and Strength of Evidence Assessment, 1st paragraph; Box B-3; Chapter 7 › Chapter Highlights
evidence.extracted: Method, wording of conclusions: evidence was privileged in the order randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies, case-control studies, with case series only when nothing better; the committee notes that this order does not imply the size of an observed effect. The weight of evidence was decided in private deliberations of committee subgroups. Box B-3 defines substantial (several supportive findings from good-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings), moderate (several from good- to fair-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings; limitations including chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out), limited (fair-quality studies or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion; significant uncertainty) and no or insufficient (mixed findings, a single poor study, or not studied). The Chapter 7 highlight predicts that stopping will probably reduce chronic cough and phlegm, causal wording over Conclusion 7-3(b), which grades only an association from cohorts with loss to follow-up. Appendix B does not place cross-sectional studies, the commonest design in Chapter 7, in its order of evidence.

evidence.locator: An Urgent Call for Change in Cannabis Research › Complications of cannabis research, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Tobacco and other co-occurring use: about 70% of people who use cannabis also smoke tobacco and cannabis is often combined with tobacco in cannabis cigarettes (reference 33, a 2016 review); statistically controlling for tobacco use can potentially remove valuable variance associated with cannabis use, which raises the question of how to balance specificity with generalisability; the same problem holds for ADHD, depression and anxiety. The authors suggest control groups with specific comorbidities and longitudinal extensions of existing studies.

risk_of_bias.note: Symptoms: pooled studies of mostly moderate risk of bias (cross-sectional pools 1 low and 3 moderate; two prospective cohorts, one with 49% lost to follow-up); ratios extracted or calculated from counts, so some are probably crude; symptoms and use both self-reported; whether the cannabis groups included people who also smoked tobacco is not described. The review is AMSTAR 2 critically low (provisional), the Ontario cohort ROBINS-E high (one question on any past-year use; matching changed the cannabis group), CARDIA some concerns (physical activity and other co-exposures not measured).

inconsistency.note: Lung function only: CARDIA, Dunedin and Los Angeles found no fall in FEV1 while Tucson found lower FEV1 after 1 year, NHANES a lower FEV1/FVC ratio (partly the higher FVC) and four studies higher airway resistance; the review's authors attribute the heterogeneity to uneven exposure and definitions, which is not a resolution. The symptom findings point the same way in every study.

indirectness.note: The symptom findings are read through two reviews (the Dunedin, Tucson and Los Angeles cohorts and the cross-sectional studies were not read here); the longest cohort is young with light exposure, so it does not speak to heavy long-term smoking; hospital use is a proxy for lung disease.

imprecision.note: Not counted: the symptom intervals exclude 1 in the cross-sectional pools; the Ontario respiratory interval (0.77–1.09) is narrow; imprecision at heavy exposure is stated in the claim as not known.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review (two-study prospective pools); not counted.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the relative risks of 2 to 4 are not counted as a large effect because tobacco co-use and self-report bias run away from the null.

grade.reasoning: Observational (cohorts, cross-sectional surveys and reviews of them), so the claim starts low. Rated as worded: an association, not a cause, and the rating is that of the whole claim, set by its weakest parts. Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1 (lung function) and indirectness −1 (the symptom evidence is second-hand through two reviews, METHODS §6.3) take the rating below the floor, so the certainty is very low; any two of the three would give the same. The biases that remain could plausibly change the symptom estimates materially (tobacco co-use and reporting bias both run away from the null), so no upgrade for a large effect. The review's own rating for cough, phlegm and wheeze is low and the committee's is substantial; those are their judgments, not this rating. Read alone, the symptom finding is the best supported part (the same direction in every study, a fall in symptoms after stopping in two cohorts) and would be replicated; the lung-function findings are mixed and the Ontario finding rests on one study of high risk of bias, so the status is mixed. The review, the committee's report and CARDIA overlap (CARDIA, Dunedin and Los Angeles are in both), so they are not counted as independent confirmations of each other.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice. All anchors are ai-located by the first reader and need a second reader. Read in full text: Ghasemiesfe 2018 (PMC; Figures 1 to 3 and the Supplement PDF not read), Pletcher 2012 (PMC; Figures 1 and 2 and the online appendix not read), Vozoris 2022 (PMC; Figure 1 and the supplementary PDF not read), the National Academies report (Chapter 7 in full, the lung and head and neck parts of Chapter 5, Appendix B; Box 7-1 and all other chapters not read) and Cousijn 2018 (PMC). The Dunedin, Tucson, Los Angeles and Wellington studies, the NHANES and SPIROMICS analyses and the 2007 systematic review are known only through the review and the committee's account (second-hand); DOIs for those without a reference record are in the reader's report. Staged as one claim, as the brief asks, but it carries three findings of different strength (symptoms: the best supported, replicated on its own; lung function: mixed; hospital use: one study of high risk of bias); the rating of very low is the weakest link, and the senior author may prefer to split it in three so that each keeps its own rating. Funding: the Ontario study's grant competition was funded without restriction by a cannabinoid-drug company (Tetra-Bio Pharma, via The Lung Association – Ontario); its result is paired in the statement with the independent CARDIA and review findings, not dropped. Reporting errors found against the abstracts: the review's abstract shows intervals that its own adjusted P values do not support, and the review attaches trend P values to single CARDIA contrasts, so CARDIA is cited from the primary paper. The simple line gives no amounts.
